records.Etymology: 106. Pr. ẓugˈo ‘bell’, ẓugˈeig ‘bell; rushing or roaring of water’, ẓuṅulˈeig ‘small bell’ appear etymologically related with Kal. gạṅgạí ‘large bell (typically tied to the neck of a male goat or bull)’. We deal here obviously with ideophones for which *gruṅ-, *groṅ-, *graṅ- can be reconstructed — Nuristani Kt. gřaṅˈaři ‘bell’ — West Himalayish Bun. koroŋkoroŋ ‘a bell’ and Darma kɔloŋ ‘bell (a type)’, and also Bodo gugrá ‘bell (kind of, round, tied to the neck of a horse)’ is almost identical with below Santali. The forms are ultimately borrowings from Austro-Asiatic: — Sant. ghugra ‘morris bells, a band of small bells tied round the ankles when dancing’ and here perhaps also ghanar ghunur ‘tinkling, jingling (sound of small bells)’, Korku ghuruŋgula, guruŋgula ‘string of small bells worn by bullocks’ and koɽoŋ ‘round brass bell for cattle’ — Bahnar grɛŋ- nɛŋ ‘small bell’ and Cua graneŋ ∼ gareŋ ∼ reŋ ‘bell’, Halang gəgraʔ gəgri̤ːŋ ‘jingling of bells’ and griːŋ ‘the rings of a small bell’, Sre gruŋ ‘bell’, Ngeq krlooŋ ‘buffalo bell’, Khmu krlɛːŋ ‘metal bell around an animal’s neck’, Thavung kalɛŋ ‘a small cylindrically shape bell’, etc. Note: Derivation of the the Pr. and Kal. form < OIA *ghuṅghura- ‘bell’ (4477), for which Turner suggests borrowing from Dravidian which he supports by quot- ing Kan. gugguri ‘curl’, is unlikely. Here more or less (in)directly connected are also the following: H. ghanghan- ‘(bell) sound, jingle, clink’, OIA *ghanaghana- ‘tinkle, clang’ (4425) which is according to Turner and Mayrhofer onomatopoeic.

proposals.evidence: DEDR4460(b) gives Kannada (Bell.; U.P.U.) buḍḍa navel alongside Telugu boḍḍu. Zoller p.1003 quotes Kannada buḍḍe navel from Pinnow and says he did not find it in DEDR. The matching stem and exact sense support a qualified family comparison, retaining final e versus article a unresolved; do not use the exact-spelling swelling/testicle homonym4266. This family identification does not endorse broader cross-family ancestry claims in the source.

records.Etymology: 114. Pal. bāṭōk ‘navel’ — Ho buʈi ‘navel, navel cord’, Mu. buˈʈi ‘navel’. Pinnow (K512), who quotes these Munda forms, considers borrowing from Dravidian and he compares Tel. boɖɖʊ and Kan. bʊɖɖe both ‘navel’. I don’t find them mentioned in the DEDR.
